messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mariana, a 24-year-old Latin American warehouse worker and single woman, came to therapy after more than a year of living as if the world had narrowed to exits, shadows, and the next sudden movement. She had been working an overnight shift in a distribution warehouse when the bombing occurred at a nearby transit hub, close enough that the blast rattled the metal shelving, dropped boxes from the upper racks, and sent everyone ducking for cover as sirens, shouting, and the smell of smoke flooded the loading bay. Mariana remembered the instant the noise hit and the floor seemed to jump beneath her, but she also knew there were stretches of that night she could not recover no matter how hard she tried. She could picture fragments — a torn poster, someone screaming in Spanish, her own hands gripping the edge of a pallet — yet large pieces remained missing. What she did remember came with a rush of rage so sharp it startled her; she would think of the people who caused it, and her body would tighten as if it still needed to fight them. Even now, she could not find the words to explain the event clearly, and when asked about it she often went quiet, not because she did not know what happened, but because the memory felt too broken and too hot to say out loud.

Afterward, Mariana began to treat the world as a dangerous place that could turn violent without warning. She became convinced she had to be on guard all the time, and that belief shaped almost everything she did. At work she kept her head down, avoided eye contact with coworkers and supervisors, and stood where she could see both the warehouse doors and the rows of forklifts. When a pallet jack clanged or a coworker came up behind her quickly, she felt immediately on edge, her heart jumping before she could even think. Night was especially difficult; after dark the warehouse lights and long aisles made her feel exposed, and on her commute home she would scan parking lots, bus stops, and storefront reflections for anything out of place. She had come to believe that her own body could not be trusted either, because it reacted before she could reason with it — flinching, tensing, and going rigid in response to ordinary movements — and this only deepened her sense that danger was everywhere.

Those reactions did not stay separate from the memory of the bombing; they fed it and were fed by it. The more Mariana felt the world closing in around her, the more she reached for ways to get through the day without fully being there. She found herself deliberately trying to leave her body during stressful moments, blanking out while stacking boxes or standing in line at the store, as though disconnecting might keep her safe. The more she checked her surroundings and stayed braced for sudden movement, the more the warehouse, the street, and her apartment building seemed to confirm that threat was constant. That constant scanning also left her less anchored when something did happen — a shout across the loading dock, a cart rolling too fast, a door slamming — and the shock would throw her back into pieces of the original event: the noise, the confusion, the missing time. In those moments she would feel the old rage flare up again, but still be unable to put the experience into words, only into body memory and fragments.

Over the months, these habits hardened into a way of living that made her feel briefly safer but increasingly trapped. By avoiding eye contact and staying mentally far away, Mariana also found herself more isolated from coworkers who had once tried to include her in breaks or conversation, and she began to tell herself that no one could really understand what she had lived through. Because she was always watching for danger, every day seemed to supply fresh evidence that the world was unsafe and her body unreliable. The more she withdrew and monitored, the more alert and frightened she felt; the more frightened she felt, the more she withdrew. By the time she sought help, she was exhausted by the constant strain of night vigilance, jumpiness, and the effort of holding herself together at work. What finally brought Mariana in was the realization that she was no longer simply remembering the bombing — she was organizing her entire life around preventing it from happening again — and she was afraid she would stay locked in that state forever unless she could learn how to feel safe again without needing to disappear from herself.
